elements.text: Foreword

elements.label: text
elements.text: Accuracy in tailoring details is absolutely essential in securing a well-made garment. Short cuts will hinder the achievement of such a goal. Much of the work involved in a tailored garment is hidden from the eye, but it is important. Sufficient time should be allowed for the construction of a

elements.label: text
elements.text: tailored garment, for it cannot be made as quickly as a dress. Accuracy in detail, frequent comparison between the two sides, and careful workmanship will be justified, for the finished garment quickly shows up any carelessness.

elements.label: text
elements.text: The following instructions are planned in sequence in so far as is possible, to guide the home sewer in the construction of a suit, a coat, or slacks. Not all instructions in basic sewing can be included in this manual, since there are adequate texts already available. This manual, with its illustrations, should assist one in developing better constructions in tailoring, give one an appreciation of what goes into a custom-made garment, and aid one in the selection of future ready-made suits, coats, and slacks.

elements.text: Shrinking

elements.label: text
elements.text: All wool fabrics, whether labeled preshrunk or not, should be shrunk before being made into a garment. Each end of fabric must be torn or cut along the thread before shrinking to save loss of yardage. This may be suggested to the clerk when purchasing fabric.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Open up fabric and press along crease. After being pressed, the fabric will still be slightly damp; spread it smoothly on cutting table to dry thoroughly, having both cross and length grains parallel to table edges.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Wet one half of a sheet and wring out; then fold the dry end into the wet end and wring again until the sheet is evenly damp all over.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Canvas, linen tape, grosgrain belting:

elements.label: text
elements.text: To shrink canvas, fold the material loosely back and forth like an accordion and submerge into container of hot water, allowing to stand until cold.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Smooth out the sheet on cutting table.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Lay the folded wool along the edge of wet sheet and fold the remaining sheet width over the top of the wool.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Remove from water bath, strip water out by hand, roll in cloth or spread smoothly on flat surface to dry partially before ironing.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Loosely fold the sheet and wool together and allow to stand at least six hours, preferably overnight.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Do not wring out the materials from water bath; this causes wrinkles which are difficult to iron out.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Remove wool from sheet, and while damp pull it diagonally into shape until the folded edges and ends of wool lie square with the table.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Keep the grain of material parallel with table edges while ironing.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Loosely woven woolens will not need to be pressed and may be left to dry on table.

elements.label: text
elements.text: To prevent the filling in canvas from adhering to the iron, place a piece of tissue or thin wrapping paper over the wet canvas while ironing.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Smooth, closely woven woolens will need pressing. Place on broad pressing table with fabric squared to edges.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Linen tape and grosgrain belting may be placed in the same water bath with the canvas and stripped through the fingers to remove excess water. When partially dry, press parallel to a yardstick to prevent curves in the tape.

elements.label: text
elements.text: With warm iron press lightly with the length grain, but not over the center fold as this causes a sharp crease.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Turn material over and press second side.

elements.text: Adhesive Paper Dress Form

elements.label: text
elements.text: Because it is difficult for a person to fit herself, and a fitter is not always available, a dress form the exact duplicate of one’s figure is almost essential. One that is made on the individual is more satisfactory and less expensive than the commercially made form. For that reason, the instructions for making a form have been included in this tailoring manual.

elements.text: To eliminate any hazards in construction, it is wise to construct a muslin jacket or upper part of a coat before cutting into the fabric itself. In a coat of princess lines, the entire garment should be made first in muslin. Although this method takes somewhat longer in the construction process, it is justified because it eliminates the possibility of mistakes likely to occur with even the most careful sewer.

The muslin garment is fitted as accurately as the garment itself. The collar and both sleeves are fitted into the garment.

elements.text: Final Steaming

elements.label: text
elements.text: A tailor or dry cleaner has adequate equipment which is not available to everyone. It is recommended that the finished garment be taken for a final steaming to be done by a tailor or dry cleaner. However, the operator should be warned that it is a newly made garment and that great pains should be taken when steaming. These operators have been found to be most co-operative and the appearance achieved is well worth the added cost. In fact this final steaming improves some garments to such an extent that it covers up poor workmanship.

elements.label: text
elements.text: A professional steaming will help the appearance of a garment, and few laboratories or homes have equipment for this steaming.

elements.label: text
elements.text: During the process of construction each garment part is steamed, following the steaming suggestions given on page 5. However this is not enough for all materials. Some spongy fabrics do not take a sharp edge and are difficult to steam. Closely woven hard twisted yarns in fabrics are apt to become shiny when steamed and fabrics with a heavy nap or pile may be flattened out in some areas of the garment.
